name: Zazzau

span.note: The regnal list dates Gunguma to 1010; Abdullahi Smith thought the Hausa city-states much older than any single state.

summary.text: The southernmost of the seven Hausa states grew from rival city-states, Turunku and Kufena chief among them. In the 1530s Bakwa of Turunku took Kufena and built a new capital, Zaria, named after her daughter. Her other daughter Amina became the most famous general in Hausa history, campaigning for decades as far as Nupe and Kwararafa and walling the towns she took. Zazzau gathered captives from the south for the markets of Kano and Katsina, and was at times subject to Songhai, Bornu and Kwararafa. The jihad took Zaria in 1808; its Hausa kings held out at Abuja, today's Suleja, until the British came in 1902.

snapshots.title: Turunku and Kufena
snapshots.text: Tradition makes Gunguma, a descendant of Bayajidda, the first king of Zazzau. Historians see instead a cluster of Hausa city-states, of which Turunku and Kufena were the strongest and held authority over the rest. The capital moved between Turunku, Wuciciri, Rikoci and Kawar.

snapshots.title: Wars with Kano
snapshots.text: Kano's Kanajeji besieges the capital and is beaten, then returns the next year, kills the king of Zazzau and routs his army. Sarki Dauda of Kano campaigns against Zazzau again in the 1420s and 30s. The Kano Chronicle places Amina in Dauda's time; Zazzau's own tradition puts her a century and a half later.

snapshots.title: Islam arrives slowly
snapshots.text: The Zaria chronicle dates the coming of Islam to about 1456, but it spreads slowly and the old rites continue at court until the Fulani conquest. Zazzau falls at times under the overlordship of Songhai and Bornu.

snapshots.title: Bakwa Turunku builds Zaria
snapshots.text: Bakwa, ruler of Turunku, takes power at Kufena and builds a new capital just east of it, named Zaria after her daughter. Her son Ibrahim (1539–1566) and her younger brother Karama (1566–1576) begin the expansion, with Bakwa's daughter Amina rising as Karama's leading general.

snapshots.title: Amina's wars
snapshots.text: Some traditions make Amina queen after Karama; others say she was a princess who ruled the lands she conquered. For 34 years her army, said to be 20,000 foot and 1,000 horse, campaigns south-east and south-west, since Kano, Katsina and the Jos Plateau block the other ways. She reaches Kwararafa and Nupe and takes Bauchi and Yauri; the Nupe king sends her 40 eunuchs and 10,000 kola nuts. Earthen walls, ganuwar Amina, ring her camps and towns. Sultan Bello later claimed Kano and Katsina paid her tribute. She is said to have died in battle at Attaagar, perhaps near Idah.

Amina dies in battle at Attaagar
links.note: Dan Tafa names Attaagar; Hogben places it near Idah, others at Vom near Jos.

snapshots.title: Slaves for the northern markets
snapshots.text: After Amina, Zazzau is the great collecting point for captives taken from the southern peoples and sold in Kano and Katsina for Saharan salt. Kwararafa attacks it around 1680, and like its neighbours it falls at times under Kwararafa and Bornu. Amina's sister Zaria is said to succeed her.

snapshots.title: The jihad takes Zaria
snapshots.text: In December 1808 jihad forces under Malam Musa take Zaria. The Hausa king Muhammadu Makau leads much of the nobility south to the Koro town of Zuba, among chiefdoms that had paid Zazzau tribute, and goes on calling himself Sarkin Zazzau.

snapshots.title: The Hausa kingdom at Abuja
snapshots.text: Makau's brother Abu Ja (Jatau) founds Abuja in 1828 and walls it the next year, ruling as Sarkin Zazzau. The little kingdom beats off Fulani Zaria's attacks and stays an independent Hausa refuge; under Abu Kwaka (1851–1877) it opens trade with Bida and Zaria. In 1902, when Abuja's men cut the road from Lokoja to Zaria, the British occupy the town.

today.text: Two thrones carry Zazzau's name: the Emir of Zazzau at Zaria, of the Fulani dynasty, and the Emir of Suleja, heir of the Hausa kings who fled in 1808 and still styled Sarkin Zazzau.
